newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian interests safeguarded at WTO - government.
newsitem.headline: Indian interests safeguarded at WTO - government.

text.p: The Indian government on Monday defended itself against charges it had bowed to Western pressure at world trade talks, telling parliament other countries seeking new mandates had been forced to backtrack.
Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah told the lower house of parliament: "Our national interests have been fully safeguarded at the Singapore ministerial conference."
He was referring to last week's meeting of the World Trade Organisation.

Last week communists who back Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition government and opposition Hindu nationalists accused the government of retreating under pressure at Singapore over labour standards and investment.

India had gone into the week-long meeting in Singapore opposed to linking trade and labour, arguing that rich nations aimed to erect trade barriers in the name of labour standards to protect their industries.
New Delhi also had reservations about efforts by industrialised nations to link investment flows with trade under the WTO's agenda.
Ramaiah said in a written statement given to the lower house that India had largely had its way in both areas.

"It will be seen that it was not India which compromised its stand in any manner vis-a-vis its core interests but the other countries which had been seeking new mandates in the areas of investment and core labour standards," he said.
The commerce minister said those countries, which he did not name, "had to very substantially moderate their position in the face of stiff opposition put forward by India and some other countries".

On labour, Ramaiah said ministers in Singapore agreed that the International Labour Organisation was the competent body to set and deal with labour standards, and rejected such standards for protectionist purposes.

"This has given to the developing countries a substantial reassurance that the labour standards issue will not be used against them for protectionist purposes, either now or in the future," the commerce minister said.

On investment, Ramaiah said India had opposed any new mandate being given to the WTO to start examining the issue, and that it would prefer the matter to be first looked into by the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development.

He said the "sponsors and supporters of the move to start investment-related studies in the WTO had to scale down their position" and agree that the study could only be taken up within the WTO's existing framework.
"India has not only fully preserved but further strengthened its rights (regarding) any future work in this very sensitive area of investment," he said.
The WTO's final declaration said that it would set up working groups to study the connections between trade and investment and trade and competition.
